entry.text: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world. He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power.
entry.insight: The grandest opening in the NT. The prophets were chapters; the Son is the whole book. He is heir, creator, radiance, imprint, sustainer — five titles in two sentences, and Reformed Christology has been reading them ever since.

entry.text: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
entry.insight: Love is defined by direction. Not our reach upward but his descent toward us — and the technical term 'propitiation' (hilasmos) names the appeasing of wrath by sacrifice. Reformed atonement honors this word.

entry.text: The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, 'The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness,'
entry.insight: God's self-revelation to Moses on Sinai — the most-quoted verse about God's character in the OT. Mercy and grace come first; truth and judgment come last. Reformed theology proper memorizes this order.

entry.insight: Quoted by Jesus as the second great commandment. Long before the Gospels, Israel's law required love of neighbor — and the Reformed read the OT and NT as one moral universe.

entry.text: 'The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.'
entry.insight: The Reformed verse on the hidden and revealed will of God. We are responsible for what is revealed; we leave the secret things to him. Every doctrine of providence respects this line.
